{{Short description|Lie algebra all of which elements are semisimple}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''toral subalgebra''' is a [[Lie subalgebra]] of a general linear Lie algebra all of whose elements are [[semisimple operator|semisimple]] (or [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]] over an algebraically closed field).<ref name="Hum">{{harvnb|Humphreys|1972|loc=Ch. II, § 8.1.}}</ref>  Over an algebraically closed field, every toral Lie algebra is [[abelian Lie algebra|abelian]];<ref name="Hum" /><ref>Proof (from Humphreys): Let <math>x \in \mathfrak{h}</math>. Since <math>\operatorname{ad}(x)</math> is diagonalizable, it is enough to show the eigenvalues of <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{h}}(x)</math> are all zero. Let <math>y \in \mathfrak{h}</math> be an eigenvector of <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{h}}(x)</math> with eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math>. Then <math>x</math> is a sum of eigenvectors of <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{h}}(y)</math> and then <math>-\lambda y = \operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{h}}(y)x</math> is a linear combination of eigenvectors of <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{h}}(y)</math> with nonzero eigenvalues. But, unless <math>\lambda = 0</math>, we have that <math>-\lambda y</math> is an eigenvector of <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{h}}(y)</math> with eigenvalue zero, a contradiction. Thus, <math>\lambda = 0</math>. <math>\square</math></ref> thus, its elements are [[simultaneously diagonalizable]].

== In semisimple and reductive Lie algebras ==
A subalgebra <math>\mathfrak h</math> of a [[semisimple Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak g</math> is called toral if the [[adjoint endomorphism|adjoint representation]] of <math>\mathfrak h</math> on <math>\mathfrak g</math>, <math>\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak h) \subset \mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak g)</math> is a toral subalgebra.  A maximal toral Lie subalgebra of a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra, or more generally of a finite-dimensional [[reductive Lie algebra]],{{citation needed|date=January 2020}} over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 is a [[Cartan subalgebra]] and vice versa.<ref>{{harvnb|Humphreys|1972|loc=Ch. IV, § 15.3. Corollary}}</ref> In particular, a maximal toral Lie subalgebra in this setting is [[self-normalizing]], coincides with its centralizer, and the [[Killing form]] of <math>\mathfrak g</math> restricted to <math>\mathfrak h</math> is nondegenerate.

For more general Lie algebras, a Cartan subalgebra may differ from a maximal toral subalgebra.

In a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> over an algebraically closed field of a characteristic zero, a toral subalgebra exists.<ref name="Hum" /> In fact, if <math>\mathfrak g</math> has only nilpotent elements, then it is [[nilpotent Lie algebra|nilpotent]] ([[Engel's theorem]]), but then its [[Killing form]] is identically zero, contradicting semisimplicity. Hence, <math>\mathfrak g</math> must have a nonzero semisimple element, say ''x''; the linear span of ''x'' is then a toral subalgebra.
